summary: AEGIS is a health monitoring system that runs on board the spacecraft and works without Earth. It watches four crew members and the cabin, raises alerts that explain themselves, and helps the crew act on them. On a Mars mission a message to Earth takes up to 22 minutes each way, so the crew has to spot problems themselves. AEGIS gives them one Today list of self-tests and countermeasures, a clickable body map, and alerts that show their evidence and the limit they crossed. Every rule is traced to NASA's five spaceflight hazards (radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, gravity, hostile environment) and to the Human Research Program risks. The onboard medical officer sees each person's trends, and the ground console sees everything one light-time later. Radiation, space weather and comm delay are replayed from real NASA data (Curiosity RAD, DONKI, JPL Horizons); crew vitals are simulated and labelled so.
details: WHAT IT DOES AEGIS watches crew physiology (heart rate, HRV, SpO2, blood pressure, sleep, exercise), cabin conditions (CO2, O2, noise) and radiation. A rules engine checks every value against limits from NASA-STD-3001 and raises alerts at four levels: INFO, CAUTION, WARNING, EMERGENCY. Each alert shows its evidence: the signal, the value, the limit and its source, the time window, and a recommended action. AEGIS supports decisions and never diagnoses. HOW IT COVERS THE CHALLENGE'S HAZARDS Every rule is traced to NASA's five spaceflight hazards (RIDGE) and to the NASA Human Research Program risks. - Radiation: dose rate and career dose tracking; a real solar particle event (March 2012, measured by Curiosity's RAD) triggers a shelter emergency. - Isolation and confinement: sleep, reaction-time tests (PVT-B), sleepiness and workload questionnaires, and a private journal that stays on the tablet. - Distance from Earth: everything runs on board; the ground link has a real Earth-Mars light-time delay and can black out without affecting the crew. - Altered gravity: bone and fitness loss scale with gravity; a stand test and a landing Go / Hold gate catch fainting risk after landing. - Hostile closed environment: CO2, O2 and noise limits from NASA-STD-3001 with clause ids. HOW ASTRONAUTS EVALUATE AND ACT ON THEIR HEALTH The crew sees one Today list: tests to take (reaction time, blood pressure, SpO2, temperature, glucose, fluid intake, an Amsler grid eye check, a 10-minute stand test) and countermeasures to do (exercise, water, items an alert adds). Each item explains why it matters, gives numbered steps and shows the normal range. Results go through the same rules as the sensors. A clickable body map shows which systems have open alerts. There are no points, streaks or rankings. THREE ROLES Crew (Today, My health, Journal), onboard medical officer (crew overview, per-person trends, weekly countermeasure adherence, radiation) and ground (delayed console, space-weather card, recommendations). HONEST DATA Every value carries a label: NASA-measured, NASA-derived, measured by another agency, crew-entered, or simulated. Limits without a NASA clause are marked "Not a NASA limit". IMPACT Crews on long missions get early warnings without waiting for Earth. The same approach could help remote care, aging and osteoporosis monitoring on Earth. TOOLS Python, FastAPI, Pydantic (backend); React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind, TanStack Query, uPlot, Recharts (frontend); pytest and vitest. It runs fully offline.

MSL Curiosity RAD dose rates (PDS PPI MSL-M-RAD-3-RDR-V1.0)
NASA CCMC DONKI (flare, CME and SEP records, March 2012)
NASA SPDF OMNIWeb OMNI2 hourly proton flux
JPL Horizons (Earth-Mars light time for the comm delay)
NASA OSDR RadLab (ISS DOSTEL-1 dose rates)
NASA OSDR Inspiration4 aggregate blood panels (OSD-569)
LRO CRaTER lunar dose rates (NASA ISWA)
NASA Human Research Program, Human Research Roadmap (HRP risks)
projectRefs: DLR/ESA DOSIS 3D DOSTEL-1 ISS dosimeter (served by NASA OSDR RadLab)
CSA (Canadian Space Agency): neutron share of the radiation dose in LEO
